Ours.dc.html.title: One of ours — nothing more to ask

Hired.dc.html.title: Hired — and only then, the three things

Gone.dc.html.title: Gone, and the one tap left

nA.text:
ONE QUESTION, AND IT IS A CHOICE.

Between a packed order and an order that has gone there is exactly one thing to settle: who is taking it. So the pane is that question, answered with the same cards the short line and the suppliers use — and the act moves to the FOOT, where every other move on this dialog lives.

The list still NAMES THE PEOPLE. An earlier version asked for a kind first and then, in a second box underneath, which of ours — and nobody found the second box. The shop has a handful of staff; the obvious thing is to pick the person.

nB.text:
ONLY WHAT THE ANSWER STILL LEAVES OPEN.

One of ours needs nothing more — their name and number are already on their staff card — so picking Grace makes the act live at once.

Hired transport is the one answer that leaves three things open, and only then do the three boxes appear. They are on the same two-column grid as the choices above them, so a third field does not stretch to twice the width of the two beside it.

nC.text:
AND WHAT THE PROSE BECOMES.

“Not packed yet. Loading it from here counts it as picked and packed — for when nobody is on the worker app” is twenty words that are true every time and news once. It is a note on the act that does it, in the foot, next to the button it is about.

Once it has gone, the pane is the answer: who has it, when it went, their number, and the one tap left.

nD.text:
WHAT SHIPS TODAY.

A section headed LOADED — which is what the record calls it, not what you are doing. Twenty words of prose. A native dropdown reading “Choose who…”. Three text boxes shown and hidden by kind.

All of it above the lines it has nothing to do with, pushing what is actually on the order down the pane — and the act stranded in the middle of the screen instead of in the foot, where the eye already goes for a move.
